doc.title: Phil Flanigan interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 15, 1998

title: Considering quitting and day jobs
summary: He describes jobs like his father's sauerkraut factory and floors in Boston.

story.theme_name: Making a living: hard times, day jobs and scarce work
story.community_name: Day jobs: musicians working outside music

blocks.x: Have you ever had a point in your career thus far where you considered not doing what you do?

Yeah, sure. Not like I didn’t always know that I should be doing this, but different points where you capitulate to existence, and the raw inherently unjust way things are in life. I should be able to do this all the time, and make a whole pile of money, and have a whole bunch of friends, and like big TVs in my house and throw big parties and all this kind of stuff. But it doesn’t work out that way and eventually you start thinking, well maybe what I should really do is get a power hose and spray down the inside of sauerkraut fermenting tanks in between season, and spray the mold off the wooden planks that comprise the walls of the tank.
I have to ask, how do you even know such a thing exists?
Well my dad had a sauerkraut factory in Phelps, New York.

Okay. That was the high school one. That’s how I bought my first bass amp, my first Ampeg B15. I worked at my dad’s factory for about 2-1/2 weeks and then I said that’s it, because I was the boss’ kid and they kept giving me all the hardest stuff to do. At least that’s the way it looked to me, and I know I’m not wrong. Anyway that was just that one. Then in Boston I buffed floors in the Prudential Building. And I’ve sucked rugs, I’ve done a little of that, and —
Well that kind of stuff helps keep things in perspective I think.
It doesn’t hurt, except emotionally. It doesn’t hurt except your very soul.
Only your soul. © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -16-

Yeah, only your soul, that’s all, it only takes a big chunk out of that, never to be recaptured again. No I’m just exaggerating. But no it can, in the right circumstances, if you’re the kind of personality who is already too full of himself and needs a good slap in the face, then that’s a good way to get it. But I know a lot of musicians, not a lot, there’s a certain cream of jazz people, natural players, that seem to avoid that through cunning or circumstances. And that’s fine. I like that. I wish I could have done it.
